Abstract 28

Background: Over half of U.S. women have hypertension, a strong but modifiable risk factor 29

for cardiovascular diseases. Personal care products (PCPs) are widely used in daily life and 30

contain endocrine disrupting chemicals that can alter hormonal regulation of blood pressure. 31

However, the relationship between PCPs and hypertension has not been well studied. We 32

investigated whether patterns of PCP use were associated with incident hypertension in a large 33

prospective cohort study of U.S. women. 34

Methods: Sister Study participants were recruited in 2003–2009 and followed until September 35

30, 2021. Usage frequency of 41 PCPs in the 12 months before baseline was self-reported. Latent 36

class analyses identified groups with similar PCP use patterns (“infrequent,” “moderate,” or 37

“frequent”). At baseline, we excluded women with prevalent hypertension, antihypertensive 38

medication users, or those missing hypertension status. Multivariable Cox regression was used to 39

estimate associations between PCP use and incident self-reported hypertension. 40

Results: During a mean follow-up of 11.4 years, 10,099 women developed hypertension. 41

Frequent PCP use was associated with higher hypertension risk [HR=1.08 (95% CI: 1.03, 1.13); 42

p-trend=0.003], with a 4.1% population attributable risk. Frequent users of beauty products had 43

higher risk than infrequent users [HR=1.11 (95% CI: 1.05, 1.16)]. Moderate and frequent users 44

of hygiene products also had increased risk [HR=1.07 (95% CI: 1.01, 1.13); HR=1.13 (95% CI: 45

1.08, 1.19)]. 46

Conclusions: Frequent PCP use, especially beauty and hygiene products, was associated with 47

incident hypertension. Our findings implicate everyday chemicals as modifiable cardiovascular 48

Introduction 72

Consumer personal care products (PCPs) contain complex mixtures of chemicals and are widely 73

used long-term, resulting in chronic exposure to endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs) and 74

other hazards. The United States (U.S.) women use more PCPs than men, applying an estimated 75

12 products containing 168 chemicals daily 1. Chronic exposure to multiple chemicals can 76

significantly increase the risk of chronic diseases, even if individual chemicals are at low 77

concentrations. This occurs through synergistic interactions where the combined effect of 78

chemicals exceeds the sum of their individual effects 2,3. EDCs can alter circulating sex 79

hormones 4, which can in turn impact the cardiovascular system, including blood pressure 80

regulation 5,6. 81

Hypertension, a leading cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factor, affects half of U.S. adults, 82

with prevalence varying by age, gender, race, and socioeconomic status 7-10. Population studies 83

have shown that hypertension is hormonally-responsive 11, with sex hormones regulating 84

vascular function 12 and contributing to gender differences in blood pressure 13. While childhood 85

blood pressure is similar by gender, boys have higher blood pressure compared to age-matched 86

girls, which coincides with increased sex hormone secretion during this crucial developmental 87

stage 14. Later in the life course, the influence of estrogen on blood pressure among adult women 88

has been observed during the menstrual cycle, when blood pressure is inversely related to 89

circulating estrogen levels 14. 90

A recent meta-analysis of epidemiologic studies showed that exposure to several types of EDCs 91

such as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) and propylparaben found in PCPs were 92

associated with an increased risk of hypertension 5,15. However, the relationship between patterns 93

of PCP use and hypertension risk has not been thoroughly explored. 94

We investigated the associations between patterns of PCP use and risk of incident hypertension 95

in the Sister Study, a large prospective cohort of women residing across the U.S. We examined 96

individual and grouped PCPs to better understand the risks associated with using multiple 97

products in a real-world setting. Further, given potential differences in PCP use among subgroups 98

in the general population, we also examined whether these associations varied by race and 99

ethnicity, menopausal status, annual household income, and obesity. Identifying these everyday 100

exposures as modifiable risk factors contributes to a better etiologic understanding of 101

hypertension, which can help efforts to reduce the burden of cardiovascular disease. 102

Methods 103

Study design and population 104

The Sister Study is a prospective cohort study of 50,884 women aged 35 to 74 years at 105

enrollment (2003-2009) residing in the United States, including Puerto Rico. Study design, 106

eligibility criteria, and data collection details were reported previously 16. Briefly, participants 107

completed baseline questionnaires and home visits with a trained examiner, which included 108

measuring blood pressure, height, weight, and collecting fasting blood samples. After obtaining 109

consent and review of self-completed forms, participants rested for several minutes. Three 110

consecutive blood pressure measurements were taken via aneroid sphygmomanometer (model 111

760/ 775X; American Diagnostic Corporation). The average of the second and third systolic 112

blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) measurements was used. When only 113

two or one blood pressure measurements were available, the second measurement or the single 114

value was used (<2%). 115

From the 50,884 women, we excluded those who self-reported having been diagnosed with 117

hypertension before baseline or taking anti-hypertensive medication at enrollment (n=17,546). 118

We also excluded women whose hypertension status was reported by next of kin or defined by 119

National Death Index (NDI) or death certificate only (n=101). Women missing hypertension 120

status at baseline (n=9) or the PCP questionnaire (n=2,150) were also excluded. After applying 121

these criteria, the final analytic sample included 31,078 women. This analysis used Data Release 122

11.1, with follow-up through September 30, 2021. All participants provided written informed 123

consent. 124

Personal care product use 125

Participants self-reported their usage frequency of 41 PCPs in the 12-month period before 126

baseline using five options: 1) did not use, 2) used less than once a month, 3) used 1-3 times per 127

month, 4) used 1-5 times per week, and 5) used more than 5 times per week. For product group- 128

specific analyses, these PCPs were aggregated into: twelve beauty products (blush or rouge, eye 129

liner, shadow, mascara, foundation, lipstick, perfume or cologne, makeup remover, artificial 130

nails/fill-ins, cuticle cream, nail polish, and nail polish remover); seven everyday hair products 131

(hair conditioner/rinse, hair food, hair spray, hair styling gel/mousse, Minoxidil or Rogaine, 132

pomade or hair grease, and shampoo); eight hygiene products [bath/shower gel, 133

deodorant/antiperspirant, douche, mouthwash/rinse, shaving creams/gels, and Talcum powder 134

(under arms, on vaginal area, or to other areas)]; and fourteen skincare products (anti- 135

aging/wrinkle products, age spot lightener, baby/mineral-based oils, blemish/acne products, body 136

lotions or creams, cleansing cream, face creams/moisturizers, facial masks, foot creams or 137

moisturizers, hand lotions or creams, lip moisturizers, petroleum jelly, skin lighteners, and self- 138

tanning products) 17. 139

Statistical analysis 140

Participants who self-reported a diagnosis of hypertension during the follow-up period were 141

defined as incident cases. We conducted two analyses to examine the association between PCP 142

use and hypertension risk. First, we analyzed overall PCPs combined. Second, we analyzed each 143

PCP group separately. 144

In the overall PCP analyses, missing values in the PCP variables and baseline characteristics 145

were imputed using all PCP variables, baseline characteristics (i.e., SBP, DBP, family history of 146

hypertension, age at entry, educational attainment, alcohol use, race and ethnicity, annual 147

household income, smoking status, smoking pack-year menopausal status, electronic cigarette 148

use, body mass index (BMI; kg/m2), and physical activity), and indicator for hypertension and 149

the follow-up time estimated using the Nelson-Aalen estimator 18. We used the “MICE” package 150

in R (version 4.4.1, R Foundation for Statistical Computing Vienna, Austria) and 10 imputed data 151

sets were considered. Please see Table 2 for detailed information on imputation. 152

After imputation, we used random survival forest (RSF) to identify key PCPs that predict the risk 153

of hypertension considering potential non-linear and higher order interactions between PCP 154

variables. To determine the number of variables for the latent class analysis (LCA), a nested RSF 155

based on the variable importance ranking was considered. In a nested RSF, the improvement in 156

C-statistics plateaued after 33 variables (eFigure 1 in Supplement). Among the 41 PCPs, a total 157

of 33 PCPs including 11 beauty, 6 everyday hair, 5 hygiene, and 11 skincare products were 158

selected (eTable 1 in Supplement). eTable 2 showed the model fit indices for LCA of overall 159

product use. We considered not only the significant decrease in AIC and BIC values, but also the 160

substantive theory and interpretability to enhance the validity and interpretability of the model. A 161

detailed definition of the latent classes of overall PCP usage was described in eTable 3. 162

For the PCP variables selected from RSF, except the no use category, we grouped adjacent 163

categories with low frequencies (<5% of all participants). Subsequently, we performed LCA 164

using PROC LCA in SAS statistical software (version 9.4; SAS Institute Inc.) to identify groups 165

of individuals with similar PCP use patterns across PCP groups 19. The detailed methods used to 166

define latent classes have been described 20. In the LCA, the best fit model was selected by 167

comparing the Akaike’s information criterion (AIC), the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), 168

G2 statistics, and theoretical interpretability 20. 169

The associations between latent classes of PCP use and the risk of hypertension were assessed 170

using multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression models, controlling for age (years) as a 171

time scale, and adjusting for BMI, race and ethnicity, education level, annual household income, 172

menopausal status at enrollment, smoking pack-year, alcohol consumption, and physical activity. 173

Pack-years of smoking were calculated by multiplying the number of packs of cigarettes smoked 174

per day by the number of years smoked. In addition, we conducted additional stratified analyses 175

by race and ethnicity, menopausal status, annual household income, and obesity status at baseline. 176

Multiplicative interactions were assessed through likelihood ratio tests by comparisons of Cox 177

models with and without the cross-product of each factor and latent class. P-values for trend 178

across ordered latent classes were calculated. Furthermore, we examined the associations 179

between individual PCPs and incident hypertension using multivariable Cox proportional 180

hazards regression models with the same covariate adjustment described above. Population 181

attributable risk (PAR) of hypertension associated with overall PCP use was estimated using 182

Chen and Cox’s Methods 21. The proportional hazards assumption was assessed using 183

Schoenfeld residuals plots and tests. 184

Study population characteristics 186

We analyzed 31,078 women, among whom, 10,099 developed hypertension during a mean 187

follow-up of 11.4 years (Table 1). Among participants, 6.5% self-reported their race and ethnicity 188

as non-Hispanic Black, 86.3% as non-Hispanic White, and less than 8% as Hispanic or other. 189

Fifty-nine percent of the study participants were postmenopausal women. 190

PCP usage patterns by race and ethnicity, menopausal status, and annual household income 191

For LCA, original response options in the questionnaire were grouped into three (‘infrequent’, 192

‘moderate’, and ‘frequent’) for beauty, everyday hair, and skincare products and into four for 193

hygiene products (adding ‘talcum powder user’). 194

Compared to White women, Black women more frequently used hygiene (52.6% vs. 34.1%) and 195

skincare products (56.3% vs. 46.5%), but less frequently used beauty (22.0% vs. 41.9%) and 196

everyday hair products (3.7% vs. 42.3%, Figure 1). Except for skincare products, premenopausal 197

women showed higher frequent use of beauty, everyday hair, and hygiene products than post- 198

menopausal women (40.6%, 49.7%, 40.9% vs. 39.7%, 31.9%, 31.6%, respectively). Additionally, 199

groups with higher income levels had a higher proportion of women who frequently used PCPs, 200

except for hygiene products. Obese women (BMI≥30kg/m2)  used beauty, everyday hair, and 201

skincare products less frequently than non-obese women (BMI<30kg/m2), but used hygiene 202

products more frequently. 203

Discussion 253

Findings and Interpretation 254

In a large prospective cohort of U.S. women, frequent use of PCPs, especially beauty and 255

hygiene products, was associated with an increased risk of incident hypertension, even after 256

accounting for confounders and known risk factors. This is the first study linking incident 257

hypertension to commonly used PCPs. Given their widespread use of PCPs in daily life, 258

especially among women, our findings have important implications for cardiovascular health in 259

the general U.S. population. 260

Supporting our findings, previous epidemiologic studies have suggested a link between exposure 261

to individual EDCs, which are commonly found in PCP, and risk of hypertension. A meta- 262

analysis of 13 studies showed that perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA), perfluorooctanoic acid 263

(PFOA), perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS), and perfluorohexane sulfonic acid (PFHxS) were 264

significantly associated with hypertension risk 5. Similarly, National Health and Nutrition 265

Examination Surveys (NHANES) 2011-2012 data linked higher urinary concentration of 266

phthalates and heavy metals to high blood pressure (≥140 mmHg SBP and ≥90 mmHg DBP) 22. 267

Conversely, a cohort study within a sub-cohort of Granada EPIC-Spain center evidenced no 268

associations between serum concentrations of non-persistent environmental pollutants such as 269

four parabens and bisphenol A with arterial hypertension, with the exception of an increased risk 270

of arterial hypertension observed in the highest propylparaben percentiles propylparaben 15. The 271

authors emphasized that their use of one spot serum sample for exposure characterization may 272

not have accurately reflected the exposure to non-persistent environmental pollutants. Our 273

prospective analysis of comprehensive questionnaire data  on the use of various types of PCPs 274

used routinely in daily life may reflect chronic exposure to complex chemical mixtures. 275

We found that usage frequency of beauty and hygiene products was associated with an increased 276

risk of hypertension, whereas everyday hair and skincare products was not. We do not have any 277

information on specific products or ingredients in this analysis; however, common everyday hair 278

and skincare products used in the U.S. contain EDCs such as phthalates, parabens, and phenols 279

23,24. In particular, hair products marketed to Black women, such as hot oil treatment, anti- 280

frizz/polish, leave-in conditioner, root stimulator, hair lotion, and relaxer, contain higher level of 281

these compounds compared to other hair products 23,24. The everyday hair products included in 282

this analysis may not have fully captured hair products used by Black women. For example, 283

styles like braids or straightening often involve less frequent shampooing. Further studies 284

including a wider range of hair products and diverse populations are needed. Regarding skincare 285

products, although the specific EDC types and concentrations can vary depending on the product 286

formulation, skincare products potentially have substantial endocrine disruptors due to prolonged 287

skin contact and deeper penetration 25. 288

Possible Explanation of the Association 289

Although hypertension is a known hormonally-responsive disease 11 the pathobiological 290

mechanisms of EDCs remain unclear. Animal studies indicate that exposure to abnormal levels 291

of endogenous or environmental estrogens increases the risk of developing hypertension through 292

alteration of ion channel inhibition/activation, cardiac Ca2+ handling, oxidative stress, and 293

genome/transcriptome modifications 26. EDCs exert agonistic and antagonistic effects on 294

estrogen receptor 27. Given that cardiovascular estrogen receptors regulate vasodilation and lipids, 295

some EDCs may affect blood pressure through these receptors 15,28,29. Despite the prominence of 296

EDCs in the composition of PCPs, we cannot discount the pathogenic role of other constituents 297

in the complex chemical mixtures or co-exposures. 298

Strengths and Limitations 299

Our study had many strengths. In this large prospective cohort study, we not only considered the 300

effect of individual PCPs on hypertension, but also considered the effects of the PCP latent 301

classes, which account for patterns of use. In particular, we used latent class models, which are 302

known to be useful tools for identifying individuals with shared real-life profiles of chemical 303

exposures in epidemiology 30. Furthermore, the prospective study design ensures temporality 304

between the exposures, covariates, and outcome, strengthening the possibility of a causal 305

relationship. 306

Our investigation had some limitations. First, we analyzed a finite number of products; however, 307

the Sister Study is among the largest existing prospective cohorts with comprehensive PCP data. 308

Second, self-reported hypertension may underestimate actual incidence 31. However, studies 309

show high concordance; for example, the Growing Up Today Study reported 85.5% agreement 310

(kappa=0.72, 100% sensitivity, 75.3% specificity) 32. The China Health and Retirement 311

Longitudinal Study also showed 81% agreement for the diagnosis of hypertension between self- 312

report and clinical measures 33. Importantly, underestimating hypertension cases likely attenuates 313

the HRs toward the null. As such, our estimates are likely conservative and the true effect is 314

probably stronger than reported. Third, we did not have information on duration of PCP use, 315

product ingredients, or brands. These were not asked to limit participation burden, as women 316

may use multiple brands. Lastly, the analyses for Black women were underpowered. Given their 317

distinct product use, chemical exposure profiles from PCPs may vary by racial and ethnic 318

subgroups. 319

Perspectives 322

This large-scale U.S. prospective cohort study provides evidence connecting patterns of PCP use 323

to incident hypertension in women. While the observed HRs were modest individually, the 324

ubiquitous and daily use of PCPs means that even small increases in risk can translate to a 325

meaningful population-level burden. Here, an estimated 4.1% of hypertension incidence was 326

attributable to frequent PCP use overall. Given that modest shifts in blood pressure distribution at 327

the population level can substantially influence cardiovascular disease burden, these findings 328

have public health significance. Future studies should incorporate biomarker-based exposure 329

assessment to identify the specific chemical constituents responsible for the observed 330

associations with beauty and hygiene products (e.g., phthalates, parabens, PFAS, or other 331

endocrine disrupting chemicals). In the future, investigating whether product reformulation or 332

exposure reduction can reduce hypertension risk could potentially provide actionable evidence 333

for regulatory and clinical recommendations. Further research in ethnically-varied populations is 334

also needed, as usage patterns and chemical exposure profiles vary across racial and ethnic 335

subgroups. Finally, integrating product use data with proteomic and epigenomic profiling may 336

elucidate the biological pathways through which chronic, low-dose chemical mixtures influence 337

blood pressure regulation. If confirmed, our findings would support expanding the scope of 338

modifiable cardiovascular risk factors to include everyday PCPs and could inform product safety 339

standards aimed at reducing the cardiovascular burden partly attributable to environmental 340

chemicals. However, caution is recommended when interpreting these observational findings and 341

additional replication in large population cohorts is needed. 342

NOVELTY AND RELEVANCE 475

What Is New? 476

• This is the first prospective cohort study to link patterns of personal care product use with 477 incident hypertension in women. 478

• Using latent class analysis to capture real-world patterns of product use across 41 479 personal care products, we found that frequent users had an estimated 8% higher risk of 480 developing hypertension compared to infrequent users. 481

• Beauty products and hygiene products had the most consistent associations, with 482 exposure-response relationships observed for both. 483

What Is Relevant? 484

• Hypertension affects half of U.S. adults and is a leading modifiable risk factor for 485 cardiovascular disease. Women use an estimated 12 personal care products daily, 486 resulting in chronic exposure to complex chemical mixtures, including endocrine 487 disrupting chemicals, that can alter blood pressure regulation through hormonal 488 pathways. 489

• Prior studies have examined individual chemicals (such as PFAS or phthalates) and 490 hypertension risk, but none have evaluated how the combined pattern of everyday 491 product use relates to developing hypertension over time. 492

Clinical/Pathophysiological Implications? 493

• Personal care products are modifiable, everyday source of chemical exposure. Reducing 494 frequent use of personal care products overall could prevent an estimated 4.1% of 495 hypertension cases in U.S. women. 496

• Even modest increases in blood pressure at the population level can increase the burden 497 of cardiovascular disease, making these common consumer exposures a potentially 498 important target for public health intervention. 499

• These findings support further research to identify the specific chemical ingredients in 500 beauty and hygiene products responsible for the observed associations. 501
